value: in Y-tube olfactometer bioassays only four of seven EAG-active synthetic plant volatiles (m-xylene, butyl acrylate, butyl propionate, butyl butyrate) elicited positive behavioural responses from adults
units: categorical (Y-tube choice versus mineral-oil solvent, chi-squared goodness-of-fit)

source.authors: Hongsheng Pan, Yanhui Lu, Chunli Xiu, Huihui Geng, Xiaoming Cai, Xiaoling Sun, Yongjun Zhang, Livy Williams III, Kris A. G. Wyckhuys, Kongming Wu
source.title: Volatile fragrances associated with flowers mediate host plant alternation of a polyphagous mirid bug

method: behavioural: single-insect Y-tube olfactometer; each synthetic compound (10 ul of a 1 ug/ul dilution, i.e. 10 ug, on a 5 x 0.5 cm filter paper) against mineral oil solvent; 60 adults per gender per compound
conditions: Unmated 6 to 8 day old adults, from bugs collected in cotton fields at Langfang (Hebei, China) and reared on green bean pods and 10 % sucrose. Seven compounds were EAG-active in flowering-plant headspace (EAG on 10 individuals per sex per compound). Y-tube results by sex: m-xylene female P = 0.036, male P = 0.039; butyl acrylate female P = 0.003, male P = 0.010; butyl propionate female P = 0.014, male P = 0.022; butyl butyrate female P = 0.001, male P = 0.002. Results: no difference between genders for any of the seven compounds (P > 0.05). The three other EAG-active compounds, (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol, (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate and 3-ethylbenzaldehyde, were not attractive in the Y-tube; their P values, and percentages choosing each arm and chi-squared values, were not read. The paper does not say whether Y-tube arms were swapped or assigned at random. Not a sensitivity measure: single dose, no detection threshold or non-detection disclosure. Same paper: in greenhouse cages and field bucket traps the four compounds caught more bugs than solvent controls.
quote: Although the adults responded to all seven synthetic plant volatiles in electroantennography tests, only four (m-xylene, butyl acrylate, butyl propionate and butyl butyrate) elicited positive behavioral responses in Y-tube olfactometer bioassays.
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces and both neighbouring sentences seen, so both ends are verified. Family and order from the paper's Abstract and Introduction ('Hemiptera: Miridae'). Crossref single-DOI lookup: ten authors in the order printed, volume 5, issue 1, article 14805, issued 2015, CC BY 4.0 vor; the Nature page prints only the copyright line. The page also gave the P values in Results (Behavioral responses of A. lucorum adults to synthetic volatiles). value: male and female adults showed positive chemotaxis in Y-tube tests toward volatiles from Cinnamomum camphora and negative chemotaxis toward volatiles from C. chekiangensis or Phoebe chekiangensis
units: categorical (Y-tube response rate versus air control, chi-squared)

source.authors: Cong Chen, Zhaoyan Lin, Jingyi Du, Jingyi Huang, Chunmei Ling, Jianfeng Chen
source.title: Olfactory Selection Preferences of Pagiophloeus tsushimanus (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) Adults Toward Lauraceae Plants

method: behavioural: glass Y-tube olfactometer (4 cm inner diameter, 20 cm arms at 60 degrees, 40 cm main arm, 300 mL/min airflow); five two-year-old twigs of about 10 cm per arm against an empty-bottle air control; three repetitions of 12 adults (6 female, 6 male) per comparison; arms reversed after each test
conditions: Results section 3.3.1 against air: C. camphora attracted females (chi2 = 5.974, p < 0.01) and males (chi2 = 4.010, p < 0.05); females did not respond to C. chekiangensis (chi2 = 0.724) or P. chekiangensis (chi2 = 1.290) twigs (both p > 0.05). Larvae and pupae collected from 15-year-old camphor trees in southern China (sites and dates not given) and reared in the laboratory; adults emerging on the same day were selected and starved 24 h. Tested at 2000 lx, 26 +/- 1 C; time of day not stated; arm reversal described but no randomisation procedure. Same Results section 3.3.1: males responded significantly less to C. chekiangensis and P. chekiangensis twigs than to air (the male chi2 is printed as 4.010 for both, which looks like a reporting error), and plant-versus-plant tests preferred C. camphora over both (e.g. females v C. chekiangensis chi2 = 11.227) with C. chekiangensis against P. chekiangensis null (females chi2 = 0.502, males chi2 = 0.020); no sex differences were significant. The Abstract sentence quoted says both sexes had a negative chemotaxis to the two other species, which the female nulls in Results do not show. Single-compound Y-tube tests (section 3.5): linalool attracted both sexes (chi2 = 6.237 and 4.163, p < 0.05), beta-caryophyllene was null (chi2 = 1.147 and 1.029), alpha-phellandrene and trans-nerolidol were avoided by both sexes. Choice and no-choice feeding tests: both sexes fed most on C. camphora, with C. chekiangensis and P. chekiangensis not differing from each other. Odour preference at one distance, not a detection threshold.
quote: The Y-shaped olfactometer experiments and electroantennography measurements results showed that male and female adults of P. tsushimanus had a positive chemotaxis towards volatiles released by C. camphora and a negative chemotaxis towards volatiles released by C. chekiangensis or P. chekiangensis.
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces (start and end seen); the chi-squared figures in conditions come from Results section 3.3.1, read in pieces, and are not part of the quote. Family and order from the paper (title and Taxonomy line: Coleoptera: Curculionidae). Crossref single-DOI lookup: six authors in the order printed, volume 14, issue 11, article 1517, issued 2024, CC BY 4.0 vor; MDPI page prints CC BY 3.0. Not on main or any desk branch (grep of Pagiophloeus, the DOI and life14111517 across the whole docs tree and desk branches).

value: laboratory-reared females preferred UV light at 50 to 1000 uW/cm2 over darkness in a Y-maze and showed no significant preference between UV and darkness at 1500 uW/cm2
units: categorical (UV versus dark choice by irradiance, uW/cm2)

source.authors: Xinyi Liu, Guoqiang Zhao, Hui Liu, Yuxuan Mao, Meng Xu, Jing Wu, Lijiao Li, Zongzhao Zhai, Pa Wu
source.title: Elimination of Ultraviolet Light-Mediated Attraction Behavior in Culex Mosquitoes via dsRNA-Mediated Knockdown of Opsins

method: behavioural: Y-maze choice between darkness and UV light at graded irradiance
conditions: Y-maze assay: mosquitoes chose between darkness and a UV arm at graded irradiance (5 to 1500 uW/cm2); the UV source alternated between the two long arms across two technical replicates; at least three biological replicates, each with two technical replicates; n per intensity is in supplementary Table S1 and was not read. Females 4 to 10 days after emergence; Y-maze dimensions, dark adaptation and time of day for the Y-maze are not stated in the text (the video assay was run between ZT6 and ZT12). Wavelength 345 nm is implied by Section 3.1 ('abovementioned experiments'), not stated in the Y-maze Methods. Laboratory colonies: Cx. quinquefasciatus eggs from the Hunan CDC, Ae. albopictus eggs purchased, Ae. aegypti Liverpool strain (LVP) from a Chinese Academy of Sciences researcher. Preference tested against chance with a one-sample t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test; the Results sentence gives no preference indices or P values (the statistics sit in the Figure 1 legend, not read). Same Section 3.1: Ae. aegypti LVP was more sensitive, preferring 5 to 50 uW/cm2 and showing no significant preference at 150, 500 or 1000 uW/cm2; field-collected Cx. quinquefasciatus preferred UV below 1000 uW/cm2 with no significant phototaxis at 1500 uW/cm2. Silencing four Ae. aegypti opsins left UV attraction unchanged, whereas Cx. quinquefasciatus CqOpsin3, 5 and 6 knockdown (dsGFP injected controls, 1 ug dsRNA per mosquito) reduced or abolished attraction; this record does not use the knockdown results. Preference against darkness only; no other light colour was offered.
quote: Laboratory-reared Cx. quinquefasciatus and Ae. albopictus consistently preferred UV light at intensities ranging from 50 μW/cm2 to 1000 μW/cm2 over darkness, but did not show a significant preference between darkness and UV light at 1500 μW/cm2 …
note: One sentence supports both species lines, each value stated in the clause naming both. Quote read in three abutting pieces with its start (subject) and end seen, and the sentences before and after it; the trailing '([Figure 1]B,C).' is cut and marked. Family and order taken from main for the same species (Culicidae, Diptera; GBIF accepted in gbif-names.tsv). value: preferred body temperature in a laboratory thermal gradient was higher than field body temperature

source.authors: Ana E. Victorica Erostarbe, Franco Valdez Ovallez, José M. Sánchez, Yamila Méndez Osorio, Rodrigo Gómez Alés
source.title: Thermophysiology and Locomotor Performance of the Andean Lizard Phymaturus williamsi: Vulnerable to Rising Temperatures?

method: behavioural: single lizards in a laboratory thermal gradient (terraria of 150 x 45 x 80 cm, linear gradient of 17 to 45 C from infrared lamps of different wattages at varying heights); cloacal ultrafine thermocouples (1 mm) taped in place and logged every 5 min for a 3 h trial during 11:00 to 18:00; mean Tpref per individual, set-point range from the 25 to 75 % interquartile range
conditions: n = 16 wild-caught lizards from Quebrada La Puerta, Calingasta Department, San Juan Province, Argentina (2878 m), caught in October to November 2014 (spring); individually housed at 24 C, trials 3 to 4 days after capture within 8 days of captivity; sex was determined but the sex ratio and any sex effect are not reported (the authors say sex effects cannot be ruled out). Tpref 35.3 C (Figure 2 caption) with a set-point range of 34 to 36.8 C; the mean +/- SD in Table 1 was not read. Field Tb averaged 32.20 +/- 3.24 C in the same season; Tpref was significantly higher than field Tb (Wilcoxon signed-rank T = 16, p < 0.01). Same abstract: thermoregulatory effectiveness E = 0.83; thermal tolerance range 35.41 C; optimal temperatures for locomotor performance were lower than Tpref, so the thermal coadaptation hypothesis was not supported. Exact lamp positions not given. Thermal preference in one gradient, not a thermal sensitivity or detection threshold.
quote: P. williamsi exhibited a preferred temperature higher than field body temperatures, together with high thermoregulatory effectiveness (E = 0.83) and a broad thermal tolerance range (TT = 35.41 °C).
note: Sentence read whole in two abutting pieces, with the preceding and following sentences seen, so both ends are verified; the numbers in conditions come from Results 3.1 and the Figure 2 caption read in pieces. Family and order: Reptile Database page for Phymaturus williamsi Lobo, Laspiur & Acosta, 2013 (Liolaemidae, Squamata, valid current name); the paper itself names Liolaemidae. Crossref single-DOI lookup: five authors in the order printed, volume 15, issue 9, article 729, issued 2026, CC BY 4.0 vor; MDPI page prints CC BY 3.0. Not on main or any desk branch (grep of Phymaturus williamsi and the DOI across the whole docs tree and desk branches; P. tenebrosus is a different species).
